### String Art (`lumenary:string-art`, models this process)

_From: Mathematical teaching and craft; when: Curve stitching in the 1860s, computed portraits from 2016; works best on: High contrast portraits._

A single thread wound back and forth between nails can render a face, because every pass of the thread darkens the path it covers a little, and many thin lines add up to tone. The trick is choosing the next nail so that each pass lands on the darkest part still unpainted.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Turn the picture into a target on a 240-pixel grid, where T = (1 − L)^1.2 for dark thread on a light board, or L^1.2 for pale thread on black.
2. Place the nails on a circle or along the frame.
3. From the current nail, test every other nail, skipping the nearest two on each side, and measure the mean target along each straight line.
4. Pick the best, halve the score of any path used before, wind the thread there and subtract the thread strength from the target along the line.
5. Stop at the chosen thread length or when no line scores above 0.012.

**The maths:**

$$j^{*}=\arg\max_{j}\ \frac{1}{\ell_{ij}}\sum_{\mathbf x\in\text{line}(i,\,j)}T(\mathbf x),\qquad T=\begin{cases}(1-L)^{1.2}&\text{dark thread}\\ L^{1.2}&\text{pale thread}\end{cases}$$

_The next nail j from the current nail i; ℓ is the length of the line in grid steps._ (primitives: tone-curve)

$$T(\mathbf x)\leftarrow\max\big(0,\ T(\mathbf x)-s\big)\quad\text{along the chosen line}$$

_The target is used up by the thread laid down._ (written for this model: specific)

$$\tau_k=(1-a)^{k}$$

_Light that survives k overlapping threads of opacity a, the reason overlapping threads build tone._ (primitives: multiply-blend)

**Dials:** `shape` (Board) = "round" (round, frame); `nails` (Nails) = 180 [60 to 300]; `lines` (Thread length) = 3000 [400 to 5000]; `strength` (Thread opacity) = 18 [5 to 40]; `colour` (Thread) = "picture" (picture, ink, white); `nailDots` (Show nails) = true.

**History:** Mary Everest Boole, a mathematics teacher, introduced curve stitching with cards and thread in the 1860s to teach geometry. Nail and thread pictures became a craft in the twentieth century. In 2016 the artist Petros Vrellis published a portrait made with a single thread around a circular loom, which started a wave of programs that find the thread path.
